source.title: All Circuits Lead to Rome: Rethinking Functional Anisotropy in Circuit and Sheaf Discovery for LLMs
source.authors: Xi Chen; Ming-Yu Jin; Jing-Cheng Niu; Yu-Tong Yin; Jin-Man Zhao; Bang-Wei Guo; Dimitris N. Metaxas; Zhao-Ran Wang; Yu-Tao Yue; Gerald Penn

page_placements.theme: Redundant parallel pathways rather than active compensation: removing one component, edge or layer changes little, removing several together changes much

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses the Hydra effect as a distinct prior phenomenon, but its experiments do not test whether ablation triggers downstream compensation or whether ablation-based effects differ from direct component effects.
record.gate_note: The paper reports edge-ablation results for IOI in Table 7, but does not measure downstream component outputs or compare direct and total effects. The Hydra discussion is about prior work; the paper characterizes its own finding as a different, normally active alternative-circuit regime.
record.test_reason: The paper discusses the Hydra effect and backup heads only as prior work, and contrasts its own finding with them: multiple low-overlap sheaves that are active during normal operation. None of its experiments ablates a head or layer and measures whether downstream components compensate. It reports no direct-versus-total effect comparisons and no measure of downstream component output. Table 7 removes residual-stream edges of a three-edge IOI core in GPT-2 Small and reports only task accuracy. That shows redundancy, not self-repair.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the Functional Anisotropy Hypothesis fails: one task can be supported by many faithful, sparse, low-overlap circuits or sheaves, and even an ultra-sparse three-edge IOI sheaf has no individually indispensable edges. They contrast this normally active multiplicity with ablation-triggered backup mechanisms such as the Hydra effect. They also propose a Distributive Dense Circuit Hypothesis, with a superposition-based existence theorem for low-overlap faithful circuits.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments discover and evaluate task-supporting subgraphs; they do not apply the original self-repair ablation-and-measurement method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that discovered circuits vary with ACDC traversal order, IOI prompt names for EAP, objective choice for Edge Pruning, random initialization, and use of OASR.

fits_no_version.finding: In the full GPT-2 Small model, removing any single edge of the three-edge IOI core leaves accuracy at 99.8–99.9%. Removing two or all three edges drops it to about 31%. Separately, DiscoGP finds many sparse, high-accuracy IOI sheaves with near-chance edge overlap (IoU 4.1%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task behaviour in small LMs is carried by multiple redundant, simultaneously active subgraphs. Single edges of a sparse core are not indispensable in the full model. This is redundancy measured by accuracy, not a measured downstream compensation response.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 306, 2026)
record.problems: The relevant ablation results are for residual-stream edges in the IOI task, not heads or layers; the paper does not measure downstream component activity or compare direct and total effects. No uncertainty estimates are stated for Table 7.

untested.parts: Ablation of an attention layer and compensation by later attention layers.
Late-MLP downregulation of the top token and how it changes when earlier components are ablated.
Single-head ablation with compensation measured on general text, across model families and sizes.
How much of the effect is compensated, how this varies by prompt, and whether it overcorrects.
Backup heads, copy-suppression, LayerNorm rescaling and anti-erasure neurons as carriers of self-repair.
Compensation under mean or resample ablation compared with zero ablation.
Whether self-repair makes ablation-based importance scores misstate component roles.

record.verdict_notes: Leaving the rows as versions ['none'] with state cannot_determine is appropriate. The Table 7 values match the text (baseline 100.0%). All evaluation in the paper uses zero ablation of edges, apart from ACDC run under interchange ablation for circuit discovery. No measurement of compensation appears anywhere in the paper. The Pythia-160M results (Appendix H) are also only about circuit overlap.

versions.untested_parts: Layer ablation and compensation by later attention layers.
Late-MLP effects on the maximum-likelihood token and their change under earlier ablation.
Single-head ablation, full-distribution compensation, and general-text results across model families and sizes.
Prompt-level variation and overcorrection in self-repair.
The named self-repair mechanisms in the version.
Self-repair under mean or resample ablation.
Whether self-repair causes ablation-based importance scores to misstate component functions.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The introduction and Section 3.1 explicitly contrast the findings with prior Hydra-effect and backup-head accounts; self-repair is neither tested nor used as a tool.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure task accuracy and structural multiplicity of circuits, without measuring downstream compensation or another claimed self-repair mechanism.

source_check.notes: Table 7 concerns the full model with all non-core edges active, not the isolated three-edge sheaf. Appendix J specifies an equal ABBA/BABA mix filtered for perfect baseline performance; these accuracy results do not distinguish parallel redundancy from downstream compensation.
